title: Pain is a teacher
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What does a bad habit cost you right now, today?

I said that the chapter says pain is an effective teacher: to get rid of a bad habit, add an immediate consequence so you become aware that the habit causes it. The book's examples are a fee for a late bill and a demerit for lateness.
I said the book proposes a habit contract, and that knowing someone is watching is a powerful motivator.

I said: you promise to change a habit and you create accountability. People around you say: you said you would do this, and you are not doing it. In my team they set goals together, like a fast for three days or a surge.
I said that in a surge you are redefining your habits: instead of working eight hours you work sixteen, so you are constantly evolving your habits.
A student said: setting the ramifications of not keeping the habit helps, especially when it is a second try, and you need something stronger than internal disappointment: external reinforcement.

I said that you may not feel the consequence of a bad habit until months later, so you do not get the warning or urgency, and some people go their whole lives without a warning sign. I asked everyone: what are your worst habits, and why don't you change them?
What is a consequence you could add today to a habit you want to drop?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write an immediate cost you could attach to it.
Write the habit contract in one sentence.
Write what warning you could set up earlier.

check.q: What did I say pain is, in the chapter?
What did I say is a powerful motivator?
What did a student say you need beyond internal disappointment?

recap: Add an immediate cost. Ask someone to watch. Set an early warning.
